chapter_theme: What makes an army: inherited courage, unity before death, honour, and discipline rather than numbers. It fails when the king neglects it or when it lacks leaders.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: the army's rank among a king's assets, the old force's rank within the army, and the hero's rank within that (761-763); its marks (764-767); and its failures through lack of display, royal neglect and leaders (768-770).

761.reading: A conquering army complete in its parts and unafraid of wounds is the chief of all a king's wealth.
761.nuance: வெறுக்கை calls the army wealth, directly after the chapter on wealth. Parimelazhagar's reason is that it guards the other limbs of the state and the king himself. The commentators count the parts differently: he has four, Manakkudavar five.

762.reading: The hardness that fears no wound when the king is faltering and the force itself is reduced is rare except in an ancient army.
762.nuance: The verse locates courage in continuity. Only தொல் is the verse's own; Parimelazhagar makes it a technical term, ranking the ancestral force first among six kinds, above hired, allied and enemy-derived troops.

763.reading: What if a host of hostile rats roar like the sea? They perish when the cobra merely breathes.
763.nuance: The verse doesn't mention armies at all. Parimelazhagar reads it as an allegory recommending one hero over many who are not. The cobra doesn't even strike: its breath is enough.

764.reading: An army is one that does not collapse, cannot be turned by subversion, and has courage that has come down to it.
764.nuance: அறைபோகாது repeats the danger of 747: the same threat of being turned from inside. Parimelazhagar's supporting verse is a woman's boast of the men of her house who fell in battle, so the inheritance includes grief.

765.reading: An army is one that, even when Death comes raging at it, has the power to stand together and face it.
765.nuance: The operative word is கூடி. The courage asked for is collective. Parimelazhagar says the many are of one heart because they love the king, and that ஆற்றல் here is strength of mind.

766.reading: Valour, honour, walking the proven path and தேற்றம் are the four things that protect an army.
766.nuance: Parimelazhagar's 'path' includes not striking those who have turned their backs, so honour limits valour. He concludes that such men need no other fort.

positions.position: தேற்றம் is being trusted by the king.
தேற்றம் is the army's own clarity, and the good path is steadiness in fighting.
It is winning the trust of the leader, close to Parimelazhagar but placed on the leader.

767.reading: An army is one that knows how to meet the battle coming at it and advances bearing the தார்.
767.nuance: This is the chapter's one verse about skill. Parimelazhagar sends readers to Sanskrit treatises on battle formation and declines to describe them.

positions.position: தார் is the enemy's vanguard, held off before pressing forward.
positions.quote: அவர் தூசியைத் தன்மேல் வாராமல் தடுத்துத்தான் அதன்மேற்செல்வதே படையாவது.

positions.position: தார் is the garland of victory that the capable army carries.

768.reading: Even without striking power or endurance, an army gains stature through its martial bearing.
768.nuance: A surprising concession that appearance has real force. Parimelazhagar's பாடு is the fear an army causes at first sight, so display works on the enemy's mind as 744's fort does.

positions.position: Display gives some standing, though the wording itself shows striking power and endurance remain indispensable.
The army's parade appearance should be more distinguished than either valour or endurance.

769.reading: An army wins if it is free of shrinking, of a resentment that will not leave, and of poverty.
769.nuance: The verse states an army's conditions, but Parimelazhagar assigns the blame upward. Desertion and poverty come from a king who doesn't pay, and resentment from outrages such as seizing their women. A verse on the army becomes a verse on the king's conduct.

770.reading: Even with plenty of steadfast men, there is no army where there are no leaders.
770.nuance: Parimelazhagar's explanation is striking. If leaders go, the men say there is no one to witness and leave too. On this view courage needs an audience.

links.note: The same formula for two wealths: an army is தலை among a king's riches and listening is தலை among a person's. The phrase shows that 'chief of wealth' is relative to whose life is being described.
763 mocks the sea-roar of an army without heroes. 768 allows that an army without fight can still gain stature through its show. Noise is nothing in one and display is something in the other.

Two ways of confronting Death personified. In 269 ascetic power may leap past கூற்றம், and in 765 an army stands against it together. The renouncer escapes and the soldier faces, and only one of them needs others.

source_issues: 769: Manakkudavar's text is marked [#] and nearly identical to Parimelazhagar's word-gloss, so it may not be independent; not used as a separate voice.
